notes.meaning: Once again a huge crowd gathered around Jesus, as at the earlier feeding of the five thousand. They had stayed so long to hear Him that their food had run out. This time the setting was a mostly non-Jewish area.

Jesus felt deep pity for the people. The word points to feeling from deep inside. Before His great acts of help, the Gospels often mention this tender feeling. Jesus cares in a special way for those who go through hardship to stay near Him.

Jesus thought about their hungry bodies, not just their souls. He knew some had come a long way and might collapse on the road home. The people were too eager to plan for food, but the Lord thought of it for them.

The disciples asked how anyone could find bread in such an empty place. Some writers think they were simply admitting they had no way to do it and leaving it to Jesus. Others note that they still did not trust His power after all they had seen. Their doubt made the coming miracle seem even greater.

Jesus asked how many loaves they had, and they said seven. The exact number matters because it helps show this was a separate miracle from the first feeding. This time the disciples had to hand over their own small food supply.

Jesus had the people sit, gave thanks, broke the bread, and kept handing it to the disciples until all were fed. Jesus did what only He could do, the miracle. The disciples did what they could do, which was passing out the food.
There were also a few small fish. Jesus blessed them too and had them served. Mark tells about the fish separately, almost as if they were handed out after the bread.

Everyone ate until they were full. Seven baskets of leftovers were gathered. These were large baskets, the same kind Paul was later lowered in over a city wall. The miracle shows there is more than enough in Christ, the true bread from heaven who feeds our souls.

About four thousand men were fed, besides women and children. Then Jesus sent the crowd home and sailed with His disciples to Dalmanutha. Dalmanutha was on the western shore of the lake, probably near Magdala. Its exact spot is no longer known.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars think the feeding of the four thousand is the feeding of the five thousand told a second time. Traditional writers reply that the places, numbers, baskets, and details all differ. They also point out that Jesus Himself speaks of two feedings in verses 19-20.

notes.meaning: The Pharisees came to argue, not to learn. They demanded a sign from the sky. They were trying to trap Jesus, not hoping to believe. They acted as if all the miracles He had already done on earth were not enough.

Jesus groaned from deep in His heart. Their stubborn unbelief truly grieved Him. His words "no sign will be given" are a strong Jewish way of making a firm promise. He would not give the kind of sign they demanded. In Matthew, He adds that they would get only the "sign of Jonah."

Jesus left them and sailed away, no doubt showing His displeasure. Those who refuse to be convinced by plain evidence may be left to their unbelief. From here on, Jesus spends more of His time teaching His own disciples.
The disciples had forgotten to bring food and had only one loaf. That was not much for thirteen hungry men. Only Mark gives this small, vivid detail.

Leaven is yeast, which spreads quietly through a whole lump of dough. Jesus used it as a picture of false teaching that spreads and spoils. The Pharisees were known for pride, show, and man-made religious rules. Herod stood for worldly politics. Jesus warned the disciples again and again, because these influences were all around them.

The disciples missed the point. They thought Jesus was talking about their lack of bread, and they may have blamed each other. When our minds are fixed on earthly needs, we can miss the spiritual truth right in front of us. Worry and distrust of God can also make believers quarrel.

Jesus knew what they were saying and asked sharp questions. These questions show His disappointment that they still did not understand. "Hard hearts" is a strong phrase for true disciples. Here it means a lack of spiritual understanding for the moment, not that God had given up on them.

Jesus borrows words the prophets used about people who will not see or hear God's truth. He asks if they have forgotten what He did. Failing to grasp God's past kindness is almost the same as forgetting it. That is what leaves us full of worry now.

Jesus reminded them of both feedings: twelve baskets left over the first time, seven the second. He even used different words for the two kinds of baskets. They remembered the facts but missed the meaning. The One who fed thousands with five and seven loaves could surely provide with one.

Jesus asked, "Do you still not understand?" His warning was never about bread, but about false teaching. Matthew tells us they finally understood. Like the disciples, we should scold ourselves when we forget God's past care and distrust Him.

At Bethsaida, on the north-east shore, people brought a blind man and begged Jesus to touch him. They believed His touch would heal. Their faith shows that we should pray for friends and family who are spiritually blind, even when they do not pray for themselves.

Jesus Himself took the blind man by the hand and led him out of the village, a picture of great humility and care. Leading him out may have been a quiet rebuke to Bethsaida, which had seen many miracles and still did not believe. It may also have been a way to avoid a crowd. The spit was not a medicine. It was a sign to help the man's weak faith, or perhaps it loosened eyelids that were stuck shut.
The man could now see a little, but only blurry shapes. He could tell people from trees only because the people were moving. This may be how things had looked to him as his sight slowly failed.

Jesus touched his eyes again, and he saw everything clearly. This is the only healing by Jesus that happens in stages. It shows Jesus is free to work in different ways, and perhaps it matched the man's growing faith. It is also a picture of spiritual growth: at first our understanding of God is fuzzy, but it grows clearer, like morning light.

Jesus sent the man home and told him not to go into the village. The man seems to have lived elsewhere. Some writers see this as a judgment on Bethsaida's unbelief. Others think Jesus wanted to avoid a stir, and that quiet time would be good for the man himself.

Jesus took His disciples far north, near Caesarea Philippi. Away from His enemies, He could teach them privately. On the way He asked what people were saying about Him. He did not need the information. He wanted the disciples to think it through for themselves.

People thought highly of Jesus. Some said He was John the Baptist, others Elijah, others a prophet. All these guesses fell short of the truth. Many people praise Jesus but still do not give Him the honor He is due.

Then Jesus asked the disciples directly, and Peter answered, "You are the Christ." "Christ" and "Messiah" both mean "anointed one," the King God had long promised. Mark gives the shortest form of Peter's words, but it carries the full meaning. To be a Christian is to truly believe this about Jesus and live by it.

Jesus told them to keep this quiet for now. He did not want crowds trying to make Him an earthly king, or His enemies killing Him before His time. The full proof would come with His resurrection. After that, and after the Holy Spirit was poured out, they would announce it to everyone.

Now Jesus began to teach plainly that He must suffer and be rejected by the Jewish leaders. He would be killed and would rise again. He knew this ahead of time and went to it willingly. "After three days" means the same as "on the third day." The disciples still expected an earthly kingdom, so this was hard for them to hear.

Jesus said this openly, without hiding it in picture language. Peter took hold of Him, pulled Him aside, and began to scold Him. Peter acted out of love for Jesus, but without understanding, and he went too far.

Jesus turned and looked at all the disciples, so they would all take the correction to heart. Then He rebuked Peter as "Satan." Peter was offering the same temptation the devil had offered in the wilderness: a path without the cross. Peter was thinking with worldly wisdom about comfort and safety, not about God's plan.

Jesus called the whole crowd, because this truth is for everyone. To follow Him means saying no to self and our own will. It means taking up our cross: accepting God's will even when it hurts, and being ready to suffer or even die for Him. Following Him means staying faithful to the end.

Those who turn away from Jesus to protect their life will lose what truly matters. Those who are willing to lay down their life for Him will gain a far better life that lasts forever. Only Mark adds "and for the gospel," the good news about Jesus.

Even owning the whole world would be worthless if it cost you your soul. Nothing could buy it back. As one martyr said, life is sweet and death is bitter, but eternal death is more bitter and eternal life more sweet. It is the height of foolishness to trade lasting joy for this life's pleasures.

Some people are ashamed to stand with Jesus because He seemed lowly and His teaching costly. Jesus will be ashamed of them when He returns in glory with His angels to judge the world. "Adulterous" here means unfaithful to God. How we treat Jesus now decides how He will treat us then.
